Zalmunna
zal-mun'nä
n. (the second of the two kings of Midian taken and slain by Gideon beyond Jordan)
From Hebrew Tsalmunna', commonly explained as “shade withheld” or “protection denied” — from tsel, shadow or shelter, with a negative. Whatever the derivation, no shelter was found for him.

Biblical Definition

Zalmunna is the fellow king of Zebah, and the two are inseparable in the record. When the three hundred broke the Midianite host by night with pitchers and trumpets, these two escaped eastward with fifteen thousand men, and Gideon crossed Jordan after them — “I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian” (Jdg 8:5) — on a march so hard that his men were fainting and two towns refused them bread. He took them at Karkor, came back by the way of the towns that had mocked him, and set the captive kings before the men of Succoth: “Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me” (Jdg 8:15). Before the execution he asked one question and received one answer, and both are worth weighing. What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? — “As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king” (Jdg 8:18). The kings knew exactly whose brothers they had killed. Gideon's son Jether was ordered to strike and could not, being young and afraid; and the two men, contemptuous of the boy's hesitation, invited the father to do it himself, which he did (Jdg 8:21). Asaph prays that the enemies of God's people may go the same way (Psa 83:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Zalmunna; in sacred history he is the second of the two Midianite kings whom Gideon pursued beyond Jordan and slew.

expand to see more

ZALMUNNA, n. A king of Midian, the companion of Zebah.

The two escaped from the slaughter at the hill of Moreh with fifteen thousand men.

Gideon pursued them beyond Jordan and took them both at Karkor.

They had slain the brethren of Gideon at mount Tabor.

He slew them, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks.

Key Scripture

Jdg 8:5 — "And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they be faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian."

Jdg 8:15 — "And he came unto the men of Succoth, and said, Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me, saying, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men that are weary?"

Jdg 8:21 — "Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks."

Psa 83:11 — "Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna:"

Modern Corruption

Asaph's prayer that God's enemies be made as Zebah and Zalmunna is dismissed as sub-Christian vindictiveness, when the psalm asks judgment for a stated end — that men may seek the LORD's name.

expand to see more

Psalm 83 is one of the psalms modern readers are taught to be embarrassed by: a prayer that a coalition of nations be made as Zebah and Zalmunna, as stubble before the wind. The embarrassment misreads the psalm by stopping two verses early. Asaph states his purpose plainly — fill their faces with shame, “that they may seek thy name, O LORD”, and “that men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth” (Psa 83:16, 18). The prayer is that God would break a proud confederacy against His people so thoroughly that its members turn to Him. That is not vindictiveness; it is a plea for judgment as the road to repentance, and it is prayed by a man who has left the vengeance entirely in God's hands.

The second correction is to the idea that such prayers belong to a discarded era. The saints under the altar in Revelation cry “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:10), and they are not rebuked. The New Testament forbids the believer private revenge and commands him to bless his persecutors and feed his enemy; it does not forbid him to long for God to right what is wrong. The dictionary holds both: love of enemies as a present duty, and confidence that the Judge of all the earth shall do right — which is exactly why the Christian need not, and must not, take the sword into his own hand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tsalmunna' (H6759), Zalmunna; tsel (H6738), shadow, shelter; Sukkoth (H5523), Succoth; charaph (H2778), to reproach, upbraid; saharon (H7720), ornament, crescent.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tsalmunna' (H6759) — Zalmunna; a king of Midian, always named with Zebah.

Hebrew tsel (H6738) — shadow, shade, shelter; the element commonly seen in the name.

Hebrew Sukkoth (H5523) — Succoth; the town that mocked the pursuit and paid for it.

Hebrew charaph (H2778) — to reproach, taunt, upbraid; what the men of Succoth did.

Hebrew saharon (H7720) — crescent ornament; the trappings taken from the camels' necks.

Usage

"“Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me” — the taunt answered in kind."

"“Rise thou, and fall upon us” — two kings choosing the hand that takes them."

"“All their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna” — a name kept in Israel's prayers."
